items.title: 14.1.4 Magnitude of a Vector in Space

blocks.title: Numbering note
blocks.text: The textbook prints this heading as 14.1.5 (Book# 14.1.5). The book has no 14.1.1, so the portal numbers the sub-headings of 14.1 in sequence as 14.1.1 to 14.1.8; 14.1.4 here is the book's 14.1.5.
We define the magnitude, norm, or length of a vector \(\underline{u}\) in space by the distance of the point \(P(x, y, z)\) from the origin \(O\).

blocks.text_alt: magnitude of OP equals magnitude of u equals square root of x squared plus y squared plus z squared

blocks.alt: Axes x, y, z from O. An arrow labelled u goes from O to the point P(x, y, z); dashed lines of lengths x, y and z show its coordinates.
blocks.caption: Magnitude of u: the distance of P(x, y, z) from the origin O (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why three squares? Use Pythagoras twice. Let \(Q(x, y, 0)\) be the point on the floor straight under \(P\).
In the floor: \(OQ^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}\).
The height \(QP = |z|\) stands at right angles to \(OQ\), so \(OP^{2} = OQ^{2} + z^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}\).
Example: \(|[2, 3, 6]| = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = \sqrt{49} = 7\).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.problem: For the vectors \(\underline{u} = [1, -2, 3]\), \(\underline{v} = [2, 1, 3]\) and \(\underline{w} = [-1, 4, 0]\), find the following: (i) \(\underline{v} + \underline{w}\) (ii) \(2\underline{w}\) (iii) \(|\underline{u}|\) (iv) \(|\underline{v} - 2\underline{w}|\) (v) \(|2\underline{u} - \underline{v} + 3\underline{w}|\)
steps:
Given: \(\underline{u} = [1, -2, 3]\), \(\underline{v} = [2, 1, 3]\), \(\underline{w} = [-1, 4, 0]\).
To find: two vectors, (i) and (ii), and three magnitudes, (iii) to (v).
Method: add and multiply component by component (14.1.3); for a magnitude use \(|[x, y, z]| = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}\). When a magnitude of a combination is asked, first build the vector, then take its magnitude.

(i) Add \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\)
\[\underline{v} + \underline{w} = [2 - 1,\ 1 + 4,\ 3 + 0]\]
\[= [1, 5, 3]\]
Why: vectors are added component by component.

(ii) Multiply \(\underline{w}\) by 2
\[2\underline{w} = 2[-1, 4, 0]\]
\[= [-2, 8, 0]\]
Why: a scalar multiplies every component.

(iii) Magnitude of \(\underline{u}\)
\[|\underline{u}| = |[1, -2, 3]|\]
\[= \sqrt{(1)^{2} + (-2)^{2} + (3)^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{1 + 4 + 9} = \sqrt{14}\]
Why: magnitude formula; \((-2)^{2} = 4\) is positive.

(iv) First the vector \(\underline{v} - 2\underline{w}\)
\[\underline{v} - 2\underline{w} = [2 + 2,\ 1 - 8,\ 3 - 0]\]
\[= [4, -7, 3]\]
Why: \(2\underline{w} = [-2, 8, 0]\) from (ii); subtracting \(-2\) adds 2.

(iv) Then its magnitude
\[|\underline{v} - 2\underline{w}| = \sqrt{(4)^{2} + (-7)^{2} + (3)^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{16 + 49 + 9} = \sqrt{74}\]
Why: we take the magnitude of the finished vector, not \(|\underline{v}| - 2|\underline{w}|\).

(v) Build \(2\underline{u} - \underline{v} + 3\underline{w}\)
\[2\underline{u} = [2, -4, 6],\quad 3\underline{w} = [-3, 12, 0]\]
\[[2, -4, 6] - [2, 1, 3] + [-3, 12, 0]\]
\[= [2 - 2 - 3,\ -4 - 1 + 12,\ 6 - 3 + 0]\]
\[= [-3, 7, 3]\]
Why: scale each vector first, then combine the matching components.

(v) Its magnitude
\[|2\underline{u} - \underline{v} + 3\underline{w}| = \sqrt{(-3)^{2} + (7)^{2} + (3)^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{9 + 49 + 9} = \sqrt{67}\]
Why: magnitude formula on \([-3, 7, 3]\).

Check:
(iv) another way: \(\underline{v} - 2\underline{w} = \underline{v} + (-2)\underline{w} = [2, 1, 3] + [2, -8, 0] = [4, -7, 3]\). Same.
(v) the sum of the three x-components \(2 - 2 - 3 = -3\), y: \(-4 - 1 + 12 = 7\), z: \(6 - 3 + 0 = 3\). Same.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
\(|[x, y, z]| = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}\): Pythagoras in space.
A magnitude is never negative; it is 0 only for the zero vector.
For the magnitude of a combination, first find the vector, then its magnitude.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Writing \(|\underline{v} - 2\underline{w}| = |\underline{v}| - 2|\underline{w}|\): magnitudes do not combine like that.
Squaring a negative component without brackets: \(-2^{2}\) is \(-4\) but \((-2)^{2} = 4\).
Forgetting the square root at the end: \(|\underline{u}| = \sqrt{14}\), not 14.
